name: Holy Roman Empire
summary: A complex union of hundreds of territories in central Europe under an elected emperor, lasting from Otto I’s coronation to its dissolution by Napoleon.

knownFor.label: Imperial crown
knownFor.note: The crown of the Holy Roman Empire, now in Vienna.

knownFor.label: Golden Bull of 1356
knownFor.note: Set the rules for electing the emperor.

knownFor.label: Landsknechts
knownFor.note: Mercenary pikemen in colourful slashed clothes.

location.value: Central and Western Europe: the kingdoms of Germany, Italy and (from 1032/33) Burgundy at first, and later mainly the German lands, Bohemia, Austria and the Low Countries.

terrain.value: The North European Plain, the Alps and the great rivers (Rhine, Danube, Elbe), divided into hundreds of territories.
terrain.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

climate.value: Temperate. The Little Ice Age (c. 1550–1700) brought harsh winters and poor harvests during the Thirty Years’ War era.
climate.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

resources.value: Farmland, forests, silver and copper mines (Saxony, Tyrol, Bohemia), and Rhine and Hanseatic trade.
resources.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

disasters.value: The Black Death (1347–51), and devastation and famine in the Thirty Years’ War (1618–48).

population.value: About 23 million in 1700 and 29 million in 1800 (Wikipedia infobox, citing Wilson 2016).

urbanisation.value: Many free imperial cities (Nuremberg, Augsburg, Cologne, Frankfurt) and Hanseatic ports (Lübeck, Hamburg).
urbanisation.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

disease.value: Plague waves, especially the Black Death, and epidemics during the Thirty Years’ War, which killed a large share of the population in some regions.
disease.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

migration.value: German eastward settlement (Ostsiedlung) in the Middle Ages, and refugees from religious wars.

economicBase.value: Agriculture, crafts and mining, with strong urban trade networks such as the Hanseatic League.

tradeRoutes.value: The Hanseatic Baltic and North Sea trade, Rhine and Danube river trade, and Alpine routes to Italy.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate is given in the sources checked. Wealth varied widely between territories.

moneyAndTax.value: Many currencies (thaler, guilder, groschen, Reichsthaler). Imperial taxes were limited and needed the agreement of the Diet.

inequality.value: Princes, nobles and church lords above townspeople and peasants. Peasant grievances led to the German Peasants’ War (1524–25).
inequality.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

governmentType.value: A confederal elective monarchy, later a mixed monarchy after the Imperial Reform. An elected emperor shared power with princes, cities and the Imperial Diet.

keyRulers.value: Charlemagne (crowned 800). Otto I (crowned 962). Frederick I Barbarossa. Charles IV (Golden Bull). Charles V (1519–1556). Francis II (1792–1806, last).

succession.value: Elective: the emperor was chosen by prince-electors, a process fixed by the Golden Bull of 1356. From 1438 the Habsburgs were elected almost continuously.

institutions.value: The Golden Bull (1356), the Imperial Diet (Reichstag), the Imperial Chamber Court (1495) and the Imperial Reform (late 15th–early 16th centuries).

stability.value: The Investiture Controversy (ended by the Concordat of Worms, 1122), the Great Interregnum (1250–1273), the Reformation conflicts, and the Thirty Years’ War.

eliteConflict.value: Emperors against popes (Investiture Controversy), and rivalry between dynasties and princes (e.g. Welf versus Hohenstaufen). Princes gradually gained near-independence.

armyAndTech.value: No standing imperial army for most of its history. Forces were raised from the princes and the Imperial Circles.
armyAndTech.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

majorWars.value: Victory over the Magyars at Lechfeld (955). Italian campaigns. Hussite Wars. Ottoman sieges of Vienna (1529, 1683). The Thirty Years’ War (1618–48). The Napoleonic Wars.

territoryChange.value: About 1.1 million km² in 1150 (Wikipedia infobox). Lost Burgundian and Italian influence over time. Switzerland and the Dutch Republic were formally recognised as outside the empire in 1648.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals were the papacy (in the Middle Ages), France, the Ottoman Empire and Sweden. In its last century there was rivalry between Austria and Prussia.

inventions.value: Gutenberg’s movable-type printing press (Mainz, c. 1450). Mining and metallurgy advances (Agricola). Kepler’s astronomy.
inventions.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

scienceEducation.value: Universities from 1348 (Prague), Heidelberg and others. The Carolingian Renaissance. Leading scientists included Kepler and Leibniz.
scienceEducation.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

openness.value: Varied by territory. Religious pluralism was legally recognised: Lutheranism in 1555 (Peace of Augsburg) and Calvinism in 1648.

religion.value: Latin Christianity, then a split after the Reformation (1517) into Catholic, Lutheran (recognised 1555) and Calvinist (recognised 1648) territories.

languageWriting.value: German, with Medieval Latin for administration and ceremony. Italian, Czech, French and Dutch were also spoken. Luther’s Bible translation shaped standard German.

artsArchitecture.value: Romanesque and Gothic cathedrals (Cologne, Aachen, Speyer), Dürer, Baroque palaces, and the music of Bach and Mozart.
artsArchitecture.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

socialStructure.value: Emperor, electors and princes, nobles, clergy, free cities and townspeople, and peasants (many under serfdom or bound to manors).
socialStructure.source: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire (2016)

sharedIdentity.value: Called the “Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation” from the late 15th century. Identity was shared through the emperor and imperial institutions rather than one nation.

neighbours.value: France, the Papacy and the Italian states, Poland, Hungary, Denmark, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire.

ideasReligions.value: The birthplace of the Protestant Reformation (Luther, Wittenberg, 1517), which spread across Northern Europe.

colonisation.value: Medieval eastward settlement. As an empire it had no colonies, though some member states traded overseas.

riseSignals.value: The Carolingian legacy, Otto I’s victories over the Magyars and coronation (962), and alliance with the Church.

peakPeriod.value: The mid-13th century under the House of Hohenstaufen (Wikipedia). A revival under Charles V in the 16th century.

declineSignals.value: Overextension and partial collapse after the Hohenstaufen, princes growing independent, religious division, and the Thirty Years’ War.

outcome.value: Dissolution. Francis II abdicated and dissolved the empire on 6 August 1806, after Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine. Most of it became part of the German Confederation in 1815.

sources.value: Imperial charters and laws, chronicles, and modern syntheses. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Wilson (2016).

overallCertainty.value: Good for events and institutions. The start is dated 800 (Charlemagne) or 962 (Otto I). Population figures are estimates.
